extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and American citizens interested in comparative government and political history
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative, historical analysis of the institutions, practices, and consequences of aristocratic and mixed republics (Swiss cantons, Italian republics, Venice, etc.), emphasizing balances of power and sources of oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of oligarchy via foreign military service
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conservation of the oligarchy is entirely owing however to this custom: for a youthful fiery nobility, at home in idleness, would necessarily become ambitious of popularity... In foreign service they exhaust their freshest years, and return, after the deaths of their fathers, fatigued with dissipation, to enjoy their honours and estates.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using foreign service (life-guard or military employment abroad) as a social mechanism removes young nobles from domestic political life and helps perpetuate an oligarchy; thus, patterns of noble employment and military service are a structural factor in evaluating whether an oligarchy will persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing nobles and commons produces relinquishment of popular power
rubrics_metrics.description: “They shew another thing, still more curious; to wit, the consequences of mixing the nobles and commons together. The latter have here been induced to reduce their own constitutional share in the government to a mere form, and complaisantly to resign all the substance into the hands of those whom they think their natural superiors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When social orders are blended without institutional safeguards, common citizens may cede real power to nobles, retaining only formal rights; evaluate constitutions for whether mixing of orders is accompanied by effective checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a third power to balance legislature and executive
rubrics_metrics.description: “This will eternally happen, sooner or later, in every country... where the whole legislative and executive power are in one assembly, or even in two, if they have not a third power to balance them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A durable balance of power requires a distinct third authority; simply having two assemblies (or a single assembly) is insufficient to prevent concentration of authority. Assess constitutions for the presence and effectiveness of a separate balancing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal confirmations and annual reviews must be substantive checks
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is an annual meeting of the whole body of the citizens... All these confirmations are matters of course, and mere form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural or ceremonial confirmations (annual or otherwise) are ineffective if they are pro forma; evaluations should distinguish between mere ritual (formal checks) and actual, enforceable controls on officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selection of councils (filling vacancies inwardly) undermines popular sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Vacancies in the grand council are supplied by the alt-raths, from the same tribe to which the deceased member belonged... As the vacancies in the senate are filled up by themselves, all power is in possession of a few Patrician families.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When elective bodies nominate or confirm their own successors, power becomes self-perpetuating; assess whether vacancies are filled by broader constituencies or by the existing elite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship restrictions and closed franchises entrench oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is an hundred and fifty years since a new citizen has been admitted... they have maintained a monopoly of commerce, and excluded all strangers, and even subjects of the canton, from conducting any in the town.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding closed citizenship or franchise rules concentrate economic and political power; measure openness of citizenship/admission rules when judging inclusiveness of a regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens’ assembly consent as a check on noble power for major acts
rubrics_metrics.description: “In some few instances, such as declaring war and making peace, forming alliances or imposing taxes, the citizens must be assembled and give their consent, which is one check upon the power of the nobles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require popular or broader-assembly approval for constitutionally momentous acts (war, alliances, taxation) to provide a genuine check; evaluate whether such consent is regularly invoked and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provisioning and arsenals as elements of good polity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us by no means omit, that there is a grand arsenal at Soleure, as there is at Berne, well stored with arms in proportion to the number of inhabitants... The city contains a public granary, an admirable resource against scarcity, and a magnificent arsenal well filled with cannon, arms, and ammunition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of state resilience should include public provisioning (granaries) and adequate military stores relative to population; these institutions are treated as blessings of government and practical checks against emergency instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliances with monarchies that include enforcement/pensions threaten republican independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the former treaty an article was inserted, that if any differences should arise... his majesty should, at the request of one of the parties, interpose his mediation... but if these should fail, he should compel the aggressor... As this article was manifestly incompatible with that independence which republicans ought to value above all things, it has been wisely omitted... it would have become the dignity of the Swiss character to have renounced equally those pensions, which are called Argents de Paix et de Alliance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty clauses that allow a monarch to enforce settlements or provide pensions compromise republican autonomy; evaluate external pacts for clauses that create dependence or external enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual rotation and liability to change as a restraint on power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The members of the senate are liable to be changed, and there is an annual revision of them, which is a great restraint.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent rotation, review, and turnover of officeholders are effective institutional restraints; analyze terms, recall mechanisms, and review practices to judge their real constraining effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of executive, judicial, and nomination powers in a few hands concentrates influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple passages note that senates exercise administration, police, finances, nominate ecclesiastical benefices, and confirm magistrates (e.g., Lucerne, Zurich): “The administration, the police, the finances, and the whole executive power, is in the senate... the senate constitutes above a third of the grand council, choose their own members, confer all employments, have the nomination to ecclesiastical benefices... their influence must be uncontrolable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a single body or small group controls multiple branches and nominations (executive, judicial, ecclesiastical), influence becomes effectively unchecked; evaluate institutional separation and appointment powers across branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex, indirect electoral procedures can entrench oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of Venice: multi-stage ballot (electors chosen by lot and ballot, committees to choose doge) and creation of councils (grand council, senate, privy council) as means to remove direct popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess electoral systems for indirectness and complexity that shield elites from direct popular accountability; complex multi-stage elections and selection-by-committee often reduce the effective power of the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-tenure accountability and financial indemnity mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the thirteenth century, six new magistrates, called correctors, were created... to inquire into all abuses during the reign of a deceased doge, and it was enacted, that the fortune of the doge should indemnify the state for whatever damage it had suffered during his administration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that investigate former executives and require restitution from their estates provide accountability; evaluate whether such corrective tribunals exist and are empowered to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermajority requirements as a legislative restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: “Four parts in five of the senate must agree in passing a law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High quorum or supermajority thresholds for legislation can act as a restraint on hasty lawmaking but can also entrench status quo; analyze required majorities and their political effects.
